summary: A standards-track document that defines how the O/R Address hierarchy, the naming scheme used by X.400 mail, can be represented in the X.500 Directory Information Tree. This lets directory entries line up with mail addresses. It replaces RFC 1836.

eli5.summary: Old email systems had addresses shaped like a tree of folders. This memo shows how to copy that tree into a big online directory so addresses can be looked up.

questions: how are x.400 addresses mapped to x.500
why is admd always present in the directory
subtitle: How an X.400 mail address becomes a path through the X.500 directory tree.

tldr.problem: X.400 mail names its users with O/R Addresses built from components such as country, ADMD and organization, and mail routing and address mapping needed those names to live in the X.500 Directory.
tldr.mechanism: Each O/R Address component becomes a directory node in a fixed order, from country down to person, named by an attribute whose type identifies the component, so the mapping works mechanically in both directions.
tldr.outcome: This gave MHS routing and X.400/RFC 822 address mapping a shared directory representation. RFC 2294 obsoletes RFC 1836.

today: RFC 2294 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1836.

sections.title: Why Represent O/R Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 2294 defines a representation of the O/R Address hierarchy, the naming scheme of X.400 mail, in the X.500 Directory Information Tree (DIT). The abstract lists purposes including support for MHS routing and for X.400/RFC 822 address mappings.

An O/R Address hierarchy is represented by associating directory name components with O/R Address components. The object classes and attributes are defined in a schema, and a table sets the order in which they appear in the tree. It obsoletes RFC 1836.
sections.eli5: The memo copies the parts of an old-style email address into a big directory, one part at a time, so it can be looked up.

sections.title: The Hierarchy and Its Order
sections.content:
Table 1 gives the order of the directory components. An object class listed higher in the table is always higher in the DIT. Only the country and the ADMD (administration management domain) are mandatory; PRMD (private management domain), X.121 address, numeric user identifier, organization, organizational unit, person, named object, terminal ID and domain defined attribute are optional. Valid combinations of components are defined in X.400.

Each node is named by the relevant part of the O/R Address, and each naming attribute is of a type that determines the mapping. The schema defines an object class for each component, for example mHSCountry, aDMD, pRMD, mHSOrganization and mHSPerson, each with its own naming attribute.
sections.eli5: Like a street address, the parts always go in the same order, biggest first: the country comes before the city, and the city before the street.

sections.title: Design Rules
sections.content:
The RFC lists twelve rules for the hierarchy. The main ones:

  • The mapping is straightforward to do mechanically in either direction.
  • mHSCountry is a subclass of country, so the same entry serves MHS routing and the rest of the DIT. The numeric country code is an alias.
  • ADMD is always present, including for the values " " and "0".
  • Domain defined attributes are named by a multi-valued RDN of type and value; the first in the sequence is the most significant. Aliases may not be used for them.
  • Where an address has both a Printable String and a T.61 form, both must be present, one as an alias of the other, so lookup works with either.
  • A personal name uses mHSPerson, and its components appear in a usually multi-valued RDN.

Postal (physical delivery) addresses are not represented, and terminal and network addresses are not handled except the X.121 form, which is useful for addressing faxes.
sections.eli5: The rules keep the directory tidy: every part of the address has a fixed slot, and if a name can be spelled two ways, both spellings point to the same place.

sections.title: Mapping Table and Example
sections.content:
Table 2 relates each O/R Address component to an object class and naming attribute: C to mHSCountry, A to aDMD, P to pRMD, O to mHSOrganization, OU to mHSOrganizationalUnit, PN to mHSPerson, CN to mHSNamedObject, and DDA to mHSDomainDefinedAttribute. Several organizational units or domain defined attributes each map to their own entry.

Distinguished names use the string representation from RFC 1779, with the keywords in Table 3 such as MHS-O, MHS-OU, ADMD and PRMD. The example address I=S; S=Kille; OU1=CS; O=UCL, P=UK.AC; A=Gold 400; C=GB; maps to a name that begins MHS-I=S + MHS-S=Kille, MHS-OU=CS, MHS-O=UCL and continues PRMD=UK.AC, ADMD=Gold 400, C=GB.
sections.eli5: Each part of the old address gets a label, like putting stickers on boxes, and the stickers tell you which box goes at which level.

sections.title: Mapping in Both Directions
sections.content:
The main use is to take an X.400 encoded O/R Address and generate the equivalent directory name. This applies only to mnemonic form, numeric form, and terminal form where a country is present and X.121 addressing is used. Other forms are handled by Access Unit mechanisms.

The address is treated as an ordered list in the order of Table 1, and each attribute becomes the equivalent naming attribute. When both Printable String and Teletex forms exist, either may generate the name, and both are represented in the DIT. A domain defined attribute and a personal name each produce a multi-valued RDN. If only the higher components of an address are in the DIT, the longest possible match should be returned.

The reverse mapping, from directory name to O/R Address, is mechanical because all the naming attributes are unique.
sections.eli5: You walk down the tree one part at a time. If the tree stops early, you use the closest place you reached. Going backwards, each sticker tells you which part it was.

sections.title: Security and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
The security section states that the protocol introduces no known security risks.

An appendix assigns object identifiers under the Isode consortium's mhs-ds arc, using a tree branch, to the eleven object classes and the attributes defined in the schema.
sections.eli5: The memo says it knows of no safety problems. It also gives each piece a unique ID number.
